I have worked in nursing homes as a carer for years, I have seen many people pass and have washed and dressed their bodies with care.

Once though I did come across this lady on a night shift and I could tell she was just about to go. I felt it was so imminent that I wouldn't have time to call the nurse. I sat with her, held her hand and stroked her head while encouraging her to go (this is a common thing at this point, in my experience, she sure as fuck ain't getting better).

After just a few minutes her agonic breathing stopped, she exhaled and went slowly yellow then grey. I took her pulse and called the nurse. She was gone.

During that night, as usual, shit happened, her buzzer would keep buzzing even when removed from the wall (This has happened before during my time, when somebody dies but not every time, not in the same room). As the other were afraid I would go in, open the windows and talk to the empty room, encouraging her to go to the next place ( I have been an atheist all my life and still am but of course I am not gonna risk the chance that one of my grannies would be lost or afraid, I'll do whatever, even if it's silly.)

I did not feel sad because it was her time really but it was quite an impression to see someone literally get their ticket punched. I feel honored that she allowed me to be there at the most private of times.

I drove by a home health patient's neighborhood, had her as a patient off and on for 5 years, had turned her over to hospice a few weeks prior, and felt the urge to go see her. Probably not what you're expecting, but Afghanistan for me. We rolled into this village to talk to the tribal elders (long story). Anyway, I'm standing next to a few kids who came up to me, because they had never seen a US Marine before. Then I heard the unfortunately familiar sound of a bullet whizzing by my head.

This really pissed me off, especially since there was children right next to me.

I look around, and see the guy responsible. So, he bolts, and I chase after him. We're running behind houses, through alley's, and we both end up in this abandoned house. He rounds a corner and I can hear him breathing heavily, waiting for me. So, I pick up a rock, and toss it around the corner, which bounced off a wall. This took his attention away from me for a split second, and I then rounded the corner, raised my weapon, and fired 3 rounds into him. Twice in the chest, and once in his head. When he fell, he dropped his weapon, and I kicked it away from him.

Nothing really prepares you for something like that. It's fucking brutal. Blood, brains, and a look of death is on a person's face (what's left of it), when something like that happens. I never really thought much about it, because he shot at me, my men, and more importantly, the children around me.

That was the first of more than I care to count.

May I ask about your thoughts before/after being deployed in regards to the idea of War?

Absolutely! I welcome anyone who has questions to feel free to come forward and ask. Don't feel afraid to ask something because you're afraid of my reaction. :)

Before: I knew who Osama Bin Laden was LONG before 9/11. I knew of him through the African embassy attacks in the 90's, and knew if he was given the chance, he'd try to hurt Americans where ever they were. I didn't think it would end up on our shores though.

After: Pretty disgusted. Not with the things I've done or seen. I joined shortly after 9/11 because I felt a duty to protect Americans and our allies against a clear threat. I've always been the guy who stood up to bullies even as a child. (My mother got many calls from the school saying I had been in a fight) :) So, when I deployed, I was always the first one to want to go into dangerous areas.

But for the disgusted part, I am disgusted by the attitudes of civilians here in America and abroad. We were clearly attacked, and attacked first (Osama's main complaint was that we were non believers on Muslim soil. Nevermind the fact that this was because we were asked by the King of Saudi Arabia for protection from Saddam during the first Gulf War). Yet, civilians here LOVE to either say that 9/11 was "blow back" from our support of Israel, or they like to lump it in with Iraq, and call it "Bush's two illegal wars". They seem to have short memories when it comes to world events that lead us to where we are.

My other disgustedness (that's not a word, but you know what I mean :) ), is how I was treated when I got home by my ex wife. I got off a plane and was expecting to be greeted with warm hugs, kisses, a hot shower, and sex. Instead, I was greeted with nothing but a text telling me to find a way home via cab, and how I "abandoned her to go on an adventure". We divorced about 6 months later, as I found out she was having an affair with a coworker.

Now, would I do it again? Absolutely. I believe in what I did was right, and the actions of my men and I prevented them from killing good Marines, local civilians, and possibly attacks abroad.

I don't suffer from PTSD, but I do have some friends who do. I make sure to check in on them from time to time and let them know my home always has an open door if they need me.

Anything else you'd like to know, feel free to ask!

Years ago my parents sent me to a summer camp. As summer camps go, there was usually a bonfire at night with skits, songs, and whatever. On one particular night it had been raining on and off so the skits were held in the camps large pavilion instead. The camp probably had two hundred kids and we were all in attendance at the pavilion. The vast majority of the kids just broke off into groups and were chatting or playing, I was one of the few near the low stage actually paying attention to the night's entertainment. During one skit that the camp counselors were putting on one of the counselors just hit the ground mid sentence. I watched his head bounce off of the concrete and right there in front of me he just started to seize. I was the closest person to him and as a kid of about ten I had no fucking idea what to do. Pretty quickly somebody was at his side while somebody else had the presence of mind to start shuffling everyone back to there cabins. On the walk back to my cabin, I remember there being a lot of confusion and speculation as to why the night was ending so early. I wasn't able to bring myself to correct anybody, I just walked back to my bunk in a kind of shock. Once back at the cabin, one of the other kids made some sort of smart ass remark and our bunk counselor absolutely flipped shit and started yelling. Apparently, he was close friends with the counselor who collapsed.

The next morning everyone was called to the camp fire ring immediately after breakfast where we were told that the counselor was announced DOA at the hospital. Apparently he had been born with a heart defect and he had been living on borrowed time his whole life. His heart had just given out and he went down right in front of everybody.

We were given the option of staying at the fire pit to sort of honor this kids life with songs and stories about him, or to have a free day with no activities away from the main portion of the camp. I felt kinda bad about it, but I opted to go play, I really didn't know how to feel about the whole situation. In the 25 or so years since then, I will randomly think about that guy, but always in sort of removed sort of way. Every time I think about it, I can't help but wonder if I'm remembering the events accurately and why it doesn't affect me more than it does. It always feels strange to think about it rather than sad, I guess maybe because he was a stranger rather than some one I knew personally.
